Remote DuckDB with OAuth

Source: vignettes/duckdb.Rmd
duckdb.Rmd

DuckDB is an open-source analytical SQL database, often used inside R. Here it runs as a remote server through Quack, DuckDB’s network protocol. Use oauth_db_duckdb() to query a remote DuckDB Quack server with each visitor’s OAuth access token. The connection works with DBI and dbplyr. A local DuckDB file has no OAuth login; this helper connects to a server that validates tokens and enforces its own data access policy.

Try the local Quack demo

With Docker running, launch the configured server and Shiny app:

shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_demo("duckdb")

Sign in as Alice or Bob using the demo accounts. Both can read the shared sample table. Try a write demonstrates that the server rejects writes. Docker supplies DuckDB 1.5.4, matching Quack extensions, quack_oauth and Keycloak. It uses a prebuilt R client where available; compiling the client on other platforms takes longer. The installed duckdb/server.py and realm-extended.json show the validator, audience and quack:read scope configuration.

Before running the app

This example needs a remote Quack server that accepts OAuth tokens, plus R’s duckdb package (1.5.3 or later) with matching quack and httpfs extensions. The server and extension setup follows the app.

Setting Where to get it
host, port The remote Quack server or its TLS proxy; the example uses HTTPS port 443
Table name A table in the remote catalog you are allowed to read
Issuer, client ID, secret An OAuth registration with the server’s trusted provider
quack:read The default quack_oauth read scope; your provider must issue it
ca_bundle, if needed The CA for a privately signed server certificate

Set OAUTHDB_DUCKDB_ISSUER, OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID and OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET in .Renviron, then restart R. A local .duckdb file has no user sign-in.

A complete app

Replace the hostname, port and table name for your deployment. This example uses port 443 for a TLS proxy; Quack’s default port is 9494.

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_DUCKDB_ISSUER")
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  scopes = c("openid", "quack:read")
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client, auto_redirect = FALSE)
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())

  con <- oauth_db_duckdb(
    auth$connection,
    host = "duckdb.example.org",
    port = 443,
    required_scopes = "quack:read"
  )
  output$rows <- renderTable({
    connection <- con()
    DBI::dbGetQuery(connection, "SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 20")
  })
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*"),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at http://localhost:8100
# (viewers in RStudio/Positron/etc. cannot perform necessary redirects)

Run source("example.R"). The app waits for sign-in before connecting and clears the output on sign-out. Get a connection inside each render or reactive expression before running queries.

For dbplyr, use dplyr::tbl(con(), "orders"). The helper attaches the remote catalog as oauth_remote and selects its main schema. Pass schema to select another remote schema. Table queries use the attached catalog; standalone expressions such as SELECT current_user can run locally and do not prove which remote principal the server authenticated.

Install extensions and prepare the server

Use compatible DuckDB and Quack versions on both sides. The R client needs duckdb 1.5.3 or later and its matching quack and httpfs extensions. Quack’s interface has changed between releases, so test your chosen versions together.

install.packages("duckdb")
connection <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), dbdir = ":memory:")
DBI::dbExecute(connection, "INSTALL quack")
DBI::dbExecute(connection, "INSTALL httpfs")
DBI::dbDisconnect(connection, shutdown = TRUE)

Keep extensions in a directory the app can use across R sessions, for example by setting DUCKDB_EXTENSION_DIRECTORY before provisioning and running the app. The helper loads Quack inside a private in-memory DuckDB instance.

On the server, configure an OAuth validator such as quack_oauth. Follow that extension’s installation and server configuration instructions for your DuckDB version and server platform. A client can connect even when quack_oauth is unavailable for its own platform: only the server loads it. Configure its trusted issuer and audience, select its authentication and authorization callbacks, and define the scopes and data access policy each visitor needs. Quack’s default shared token check does not validate OAuth tokens.

Expose the server through TLS with a certificate trusted by the DuckDB client, typically through a reverse proxy. See Quack security. Pass ca_bundle = "path/to/private-ca.pem" if the server uses a private CA. The helper explicitly enables TLS, including for loopback hosts. For local development only, allow_local_http = TRUE permits HTTP on localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1].

quack_oauth also has client-side OAuth flows. They are unnecessary here: shinyOAuth handles browser sign-in and renewal; the helper passes only the resulting access token to Quack. It creates no persistent token secrets.

Register the Shiny app

Register an OAuth client with the server’s identity provider and allow http://localhost:8100 as a redirect URI. Request access tokens for the audience configured on the Quack server. An ID token or a token issued for another API cannot substitute for this access token.

This example uses an OIDC provider and the quack:read scope from quack_oauth’s default policy. Configure the provider to issue that scope and the correct audience. Use your server’s scopes if its policy differs. Request offline_access too if your provider requires it for renewal. For providers requiring a resource parameter or named token target, configure that on the shinyOAuth client and pass the target name to oauth_db_duckdb().

Save your registration in .Renviron and restart R:

OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret
OAUTHDB_DUCKDB_ISSUER=https://login.example.org/realms/reporting

Connection lifetime

Call con() before each operation. Quack receives a token when attaching, so the helper closes and replaces the connection when the access token changes. This ends transactions and discards temporary client state on the old connection. Keep a transaction within one synchronous operation and get a new handle for the next operation.

Account changes, lost required permissions, sign-out and Shiny session end close the connection and shut down its private DuckDB instance. A caller retaining a raw handle must still obtain con() before each operation; the server decides whether an existing remote session remains authorized. The helper never retries SQL statements or replays a transaction.

Setup errors omit the token-bearing SQL statement. An attachment failure can mean an unavailable endpoint, a rejected TLS certificate or token, denied catalog access, or an unknown schema. Check server diagnostics and confirm the issuer, audience and scopes match the app registration.

For several accounts and saved results, see Getting started.

Test the integration locally

The source checkout includes a Docker fixture with a real quack_oauth server, a JWKS issuer and a TLS proxy. It generates its own signed test tokens and certificates. From the repository root, run Rscript --vanilla tools/check-duckdb-oauth.R with Docker running and the test dependencies installed. The checks cover DBI/dbplyr reads, rejected writes, invalid tokens and TLS verification without production credentials.
